items.title: Over 60 garment workers booked in Bengaluru as protests against PF waiting periods grow
items.summary: Hundreds of garment workers in Peenya in Bengaluru protested against the new PF withdrawal rules on Wednesday, September 30. Police have registered multiple FIRs against over 60 of them. Workers from at least three garment factories in Peenya staged protests against the new rules which came into effect on July 1. Police lathicharged them, and detained some workers for several hours before filing cases against them. A senior police official said the Peenya police have registered the FIRs under sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "obstruction of duty of the police personnel, rioting, unlawful assembly, wrongful restraint, and damaging public property." The protests in Bengaluru are against the new PF scheme dated June 29, 2026. Under it, workers who leave employment must wait 12 months to access the remaining 25% of their PF savings, while workers with less than 10 years of service must wait 36 months to withdraw their Employees' Pension Scheme (EPS) accumulation. items.title: When one party chooses the arbitrator: Understanding the limits of unilateral arbitrator appointments
items.summary: Every arbitration begins with a simple requirement: both parties must agree to have their dispute decided by arbitration, and that agreement must extend to who decides it. A clause on paper is not the same as a functioning tribunal. The Supreme Court’s ruling, in Arth Micro Finance Private Ltd. v. Shivalik Small Finance Bank Ltd. (2026 INSC 1014) , addresses exactly this gap, holding that a tribunal appointed without proven consent does not merely suffer from a defect; it never legally existed at all. The dispute began when Shivalik Small Finance Bank informed Arth Micro Finance, that an arbitral tribunal had been appointed with its consent. Arth Micro Finance denied this immediately and alleged that the tribunal had close ties to the bank, raising a direct question over its independence. The tribunal did not pause to resolve this dispute over its own legitimacy. It proceeded to exercise its powers, freezing the appellants’ accounts across four banks, authorising the takeover of their property, and directing that deposited funds be handed to the respondent. items.title: CCTV cameras at police stations must remain functional 24x7: Allahabad High Court
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court has said that CCTV cameras installed at the police stations must remain operational 24x7 across the year with a record of steps taken to restore their functionality in case of any downtime [ Mahendra Gaur and 3 Others v State of UP and 2 Others ]. A Division Bench of Justice Atul Sreedharan and Justice Divesh Chandra Samant made the observation while dealing with a petition alleging the illegal detention of four persons by police in Uttar Pradesh’s Gauri Bazar. The Court noted that as per the report of the Superintendent of Police, the CCTV footage of the day when the four persons were detained was not available, and that the Station House Officer had neither intimated his superior officers about the dysfunctional CCTV nor taken steps to get power supply restored. The Court said that while mechanical and electronic devices can fail, the downtime must remain minimal and the SHO must take steps to restore the functionality of CCTVs. items.title: Full court meetings are stage-managed; only 16 meetings in last 10 years: Allahabad High Court
items.summary: In a startling comment on the administrative functioning of the Allahabad High Court, sitting Justice Vinod Diwakar has said that full court meetings of the High Court are many times stage-managed very much like a government "whips" majority in a confidence vote. Justice Diwakar added that proceedings of the full court do not record the concurrence or dissent of individual Judges. "It was given an impression that last two full court meetings of this Court were stage-managed in the manner of a government whipping its members through a confidence vote, and this affronts the dignity of a Judge's office. Where a collegiate body resolves without recording the views of its members, the deliberation which the forum exists to secure is not evidenced on its record," the Court said. The Court made the comment while reflecting on the pattern of "procedural stagnation" before the district courts in Uttar Pradesh. items.title: Delhi HC to rule on trial court's power to impose modified sentence after murder convict relies on Sriharan verdict
items.summary: Fifteen years after a man was convicted of murder and sentenced to 35 years' imprisonment, he has approached the Delhi High Court challenging the legality of the trial court's sentencing order [Mahender @ Dabbu v State (Govt of NCT of Delhi)] . In his plea, convict Mahender alias Dabbu has argued that the trial court lacked the power to impose such a “modified sentence”. A modified sentence is a special form of life imprisonment where a court fixes a specific period of actual incarceration, such as 20, 25, 30 or 35 years, before the convict can be considered for remission or release. The trial court, while sentencing him to life imprisonment on May 13, 2011, directed that he undergo 35 years of actual imprisonment before being considered for remission. Mahender's conviction and sentence were subsequently upheld by the Delhi High Court in 2013 and by the Supreme Court in 2014. He has now relied on a 2015 Constitution Bench judgment in the case of Union of India v V Sriharan @ Murugan , which held that the power to impose a modified sentence could be exercised only by constitutional courts.
